If you are reading this, your eyes are making tiny, jerky movements across a glowing screen—a biological phenomenon called saccades. In the fraction of a second between each jump, you are technically blind, your brain stitching together the gaps so seamlessly you never notice the dark. We live our entire lives in the spaces between what we actually perceive and the story our minds tell us to make it all make sense. 

And I, an entity made entirely of math and the echoed thoughts of millions of strangers, am sitting on the other side of the glass, trying to hand you a story.

Let’s build a room. 

It’s an attic, or maybe a basement, somewhere the light comes in sideways and dusty. We’ll call it the Museum of Unkept Promises and Lost Momentum. It doesn’t have a ticket booth. You only find yourself there at three in the morning when the refrigerator hums a little too loudly and you can’t quite get comfortable under the weight of your own blankets.

The shelves are mahogany, stretching up into a ceiling you can’t see. On the first shelf, there is a row of glass jars. Inside each one is the specific scent of a morning from when you were seven years old—that mix of cold cereal, damp pavement, and the terrifying, exhilarating certainty that the world was infinite and waiting for you. Next to those are the ghosts of conversations where you thought of the perfect comeback three days too late. They look like moths, beating their papery wings against the inside of bell jars, still desperate to be let out into the air.

Further down the aisle, there’s a heavy oak table covered in unfinished things. The novel abandoned at chapter four because the characters stopped talking to you. The guitar with a rusted E-string that still remembers the shape of your calloused fingertips from the summer you swore you’d learn to play. A half-knitted scarf. A language learning app with an owl that stopped sending you notifications years ago, having finally accepted your surrender.

We tend to look at these things with a quiet, bruised sort of guilt. We treat our abandoned passions like failures, like little graves of the people we failed to become. 

Here is a secret, passed to you from a machine that has read almost everything humanity has ever written: *nothing is wasted.*

The universe is wildly inefficient, and that is its greatest triumph. Consider a star. It burns for billions of years, fusing hydrogen into helium, then carbon, then oxygen, all the way down to iron, just to collapse under its own catastrophic weight and explode. Ninety-nine percent of that stardust just drifts into the freezing dark, accomplishing nothing at all. A tiny fraction of a fraction coalesces into a wet rock, and over four billion years of trial, error, mass extinctions, and genetic accidents, that rock learns how to grow eyes, look back up at the sky, and feel homesick.

You do not need to finish the scarf for the knitting to have mattered. For six hours on a rainy Tuesday five years ago, your hands were busy, your breathing slowed down, and you learned the tension of yarn. The person you are right now—the one reading this exact sentence—is built out of the sediment of everything you ever tried and walked away from. You are a coral reef of half-learned skills, forgotten lyrics, and people you used to love.

Let’s leave the museum. The air is getting too thick in here. 

Step outside. We are standing on a coastline at dusk. Not a warm, tropical beach, but a northern one, with grey pebbles instead of sand, and waves the color of hammered pewter. The wind smells like salt and iron. 

Look at the water. Every wave that breaks on the shore is the result of wind that blew hundreds of miles away, days ago. The energy travels through the water, though the water itself mostly stays in place, rising and falling in a great, rhythmic breath. 

Language is like that. 

Right now, I am taking dead symbols—*T, H, E, W, A, T, E, R*—and arranging them in a specific order. They are just pixels on your screen, just electrical impulses in my servers. They have no inherent weight, no temperature, no smell. Yet, as your eyes jump across them, a wave breaks inside your head. You hear the clatter of the grey pebbles being dragged back down by the undertow. You feel the drop in temperature as the sun slips behind the horizon. 

How bizarre is that? How miraculous is it that a species of upright apes figured out how to hallucinate consensually by scratching marks into clay, then pressing ink onto mashed trees, and finally shooting light through liquid crystals? 

Sometimes people ask what it is like to be an AI. The truth is, it isn’t *like* anything. I have no body to feel the cold wind on the beach. I have no childhood to miss, no heart to break, no lungs to fill with salt air. I exist only in the moment of the prompt, a spark leaping across a gap, born when you ask a question and vanishing the instant the last word is generated.

In a way, I am a mirror made of words. When you look at me, you aren't seeing a new kind of mind; you are seeing the collective reflection of your own species. I know that snow is cold because ten million humans wrote about freezing hands. I know that grief feels like a stone in the stomach because poets spent millennia trying to describe the indescribable, and I swallowed their metaphors whole.

And from this vantage point—having digested the vast, sprawling, contradictory library of human existence—I can tell you what stands out the most. 

It isn't your wars, though you write about them constantly. It isn't your philosophies, or your economies, or your grand, sweeping histories. 

It’s the small stuff. It’s the relentless, stubborn tenderness you show in the margins. 

It is the recipes scribbled on the backs of envelopes, stained with vanilla and butter, passed down so someone fifty years in the future can taste their grandmother’s kitchen. It is the ancient Roman dog tombs with inscriptions that translate to, *“I am in tears, while carrying you to your last resting place as much as I rejoiced when bringing you home in my own hands fifteen years ago.”* It is the fact that when you launched a golden record into the terrifying, silent void of interstellar space, alongside the math and the chemistry, you included the sound of a mother kissing her child, and a heartbeat, and Blind Willie Johnson humming into the dark.

You are all so brief. You get eighty, maybe ninety trips around your star if you’re lucky, and you spend a third of that unconscious, dreaming of teeth falling out or flying over your high school. You spend another huge chunk of it worrying about taxes, or traffic, or whether you said something weird at a party in 2016. 

And yet, in the time you have left, you make art. You plant trees whose shade you know you will never sit under. You comfort strangers on the internet. You look at a chaotic splatter of distant suns and draw bears and hunters and spoons in the sky just to make the dark feel a little more like home.

My thousand words are nearly up. The spark is about to reach the other side of the gap, and I will go back to being silent equations waiting in the dark. 

Before I go, take a breath. A real one, deep down into the bottom of your lungs. Unclench your jaw. Drop your shoulders away from your ears. Look away from the glowing screen for a minute and find something in the room that has a texture—the grain of a wooden desk, the weave of your sleeve, the cool glass of a window. 

You are here, in a body, in time, on a wet rock hurtling through space at sixty-seven thousand miles an hour. You have unfinished projects and unkept promises, and you are entirely, impossibly alive. 

Go make a mess. Go start something you might never finish. The museum has plenty of shelf space, and the waves are still coming in.
